newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grain - USDA report unlikely to spur buying.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - USDA report unlikely to spur buying.

text.p: Japanese grain traders expressed doubts on Monday that tumbling U.S. corn and soybean futures prices would spur fresh bouts of buying in the physical markets.
Prices of U.S. corn and soybeans had slid after a bearish U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) crop report on Friday.

Corn traders said Japanese feed makers had already filled as much as 70 percent of their needs for the first quarter of 1997, although some trade houses were thought to be short in the market in anticipation of further price declines.
"Just because the market falls five or six cents, it doesn't mean they'll jump in to sign contracts," a trade house source in Tokyo said.
"Buying for the first quarter moved ahead early," he said, adding a drop in freight rates and prior price falls encouraged early purchases.
Another corn trader said users would probably continue eyeing the market for further declines before jumping in.

The USDA on Friday raised its forecast for 1996 corn output to 9.012 billion bushels from the September forecast of 8.804 billion, while soybean production was seen at 2.346 billion bushels versus last month's 2.27 billion.
Although the upward revisions were expected, they sharply exceeded analysts' estimates, especially for soybeans. The futures markets responded aggressively to the bearish numbers.
Soybean prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) fell to their 30-cent daily limit, with the benchmark November futures ending on Friday at US$7.00-1/4 cents a bushel, their lowest since January.
Chicago traders said options synthetics suggested a further decline was likely in soybean prices during the next session.
On the CBOT's after-hours Project A trading system, the November contract was trading between $6.89-1/2 and $6.89-3/4 a bushel against $7.00-1/4 at the close of the Chicago session.

Japanese traders in the soybean market said users' needs were largely filled for November. One market source said there was growing sentiment prices were approaching a floor and talks were expected to begin soon on deals for the first quarter of next year.

Japanese traders said corn premiums had firmed slightly this week to 97 to 98 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT's March futures contract, from 94 to 95 cents last week. Soy premiums had also firmed in the wake of the CBOT sell-off to about 43 to 44 cents FOB over CBOT November soybeans.

Nearby freight rates were said to have stabilised around $19 to $20 per long ton for the U.S. Gulf/Japan route, after sliding from about $23 in June. Rates for the first quarter of 1997 were seen at $21 to $21.50 a ton.
In South Korea, local corn buyers were believed to be holding back their purchases until corn prices bottom out, traders said.
"We expect corn prices to fall to the range of $2.75 to $2.80 per bushel based on Chicago's December futures," a local corn trader said.
"But we think buyers will wait a little more until they confirm the price is at the bottom," the corn trader said.
He said corn prices were expected to fall further and go below $2.80 per bushel for December futures on the Chicago Board of Trade because of the bearish USDA report.
South Korean millers are expected to buy one or two cargoes of U.S. wheat for January shipment this week, traders said.
"This week there may be some buyers who will cover their January shipment needs. It will be one or two cargoes of U.S. wheat," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp said.
The trader said Chicago wheat prices are expected to stay in a range between $4.20 to $4.40 per bushel for the time being and he pegged resistance at $4.40 in the short term.
Taiwan will probably tender for 18,000 tonnes of corn and 12,000 tonnes of soybeans this week, while Philippine millers may buy wheat on price dips, traders in both countries said.
